dae498ec13ecb33364d0afa7693879b09e5e47d2.summary: ElvenPath reported on the N40 banking trojan, used in a recent campaign against Chilean banks. It is described as an evolved version of a Brazilian banking trojan used in earlier attacks. The malware relies on DLL Hijacking: a legitimate Windows application is dropped with a renamed trojan DLL signed using a black-market certificate, so SmartScreen only sees a legitimate app run. It also uses real-time string decoding, non-standard ports for command and control, and can steal credentials and replace a bitcoin wallet in the victim's clipboard. The report does not say how N40 spreads.…

da594d7b428d58b16edbf9012f948daed3c24cb8.summary: CrowdStrike Intelligence describes CARBON SPIDER, also called FIN7 and active since 2013, moving in 2020 from point-of-sale data theft to broad ransomware operations. It reports the group used REvil and its own Darkside ransomware, and launched a Darkside affiliate program in November 2020. Several links to REvil and Darkside are moderate-confidence assessments. This is part one of a two-part series; part two covers the aftermath of the Colonial Pipeline attack.

daebaf0e378fc11ad510c22584e45580cf068611.summary: Kaspersky GERT describes NKAbuse, a Go-written multiplatform implant. It targets mainly Linux desktops and can also infect MIPS and ARM IoT devices. It combines DDoS flooding with RAT backdoor features and uses the NKN peer-to-peer blockchain network to communicate with its bot master. Initial access was reportedly via an old Apache Struts2 flaw (CVE-2017-5638) against a financial company. Persistence is via cron jobs. The report describes victims in Colombia, Mexico and Vietnam, and says the malware has no self-propagation. Kaspersky products detect it as a Linux backdoor.
